messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir had always taken pride in his work as a paramedic, but that changed the day his younger brother, Ali, was severely injured in a car accident. Amir was the first responder on the scene and had to fight to save his brother's life. The memory of Ali's broken body, the sound of his own frantic voice calling for backup, and the smell of antiseptic from the ambulance still haunted him. Since then, Amir found himself becoming increasingly avoidant of work, citing excuses to skip shifts or opting out of emergency calls whenever possible. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was somehow responsible for Ali's condition, and the guilt was suffocating. The visible injuries on others, even minor ones, would send him spiraling back to that day. Reminders of victims – the way they looked, the sounds they made – all brought back the same terror he felt when he saw Ali's battered face. When Amir did go to work, he threw himself into tasks to keep his mind occupied, overworking to the point of exhaustion. His colleagues noticed a change in him, but Amir just shrugged it off as stress. In reality, he was desperate to distract himself from the memories that lingered long after his shift ended. The smell of hospitals or antiseptic would transport him back to the ambulance, reliving the trauma with all its sensory details. As time passed, Amir became increasingly jumpy, startling at unexpected touches or loud noises. He always chose seats in safe locations, away from potential threats. Concentrating on anything proved difficult; his mind wandered back to that day, rehashing what he could have done differently. When memories of Ali's accident resurfaced, they brought back the same terror Amir felt when it happened. Amir couldn't shake off the feeling that he had permanently changed for the worse, that he was no longer capable of protecting himself or others. He became convinced that he had failed to protect his brother and that this failure would haunt him forever. These negative self-appraisals only fueled his avoidance behaviors; if he wasn't reliable, why bother trying? The memories of Ali's accident reinforced these feelings of inadequacy, solidifying Amir's conviction that he was forever damaged. The cycle had become self-reinforcing: Amir's triggers – the sights and smells associated with trauma – led him to avoid work or overwork, which in turn made him feel more vulnerable to threat. His negative appraisals fueled this avoidance, creating a sense of permanent damage that seemed insurmountable. As Amir navigated his daily life, he felt trapped by these memories, unsure how to escape the prison of his own guilt and fear. It was only when Ali's condition took a turn for the worse, and Amir realized he couldn't be there for his brother because of his own emotional paralysis, that he finally sought help. He knew he needed to confront the trauma head-on, but the thought of reliving it all again terrified him. What Amir feared most was losing himself completely to these memories, becoming forever lost in a sea of guilt and self-doubt.
